title: Open files

D0.outcome: Explains that an open file matters only if a rook can use it to reach an entry square on the seventh or eighth rank or attack a target.

D1.outcome: Told to use the open file, names the target pawn and the entry square and places the rook accordingly.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled middlegame positions, decides whether a file helps by naming its entry square and checking the square is not covered; decides whether opening a file helps him or the opponent.

D3.outcome: Chooses among the three ways past an obstructing pawn (batter, lever, sacrifice) by checking whether the pawn is protected, and counts attackers against defenders on it; uses a closed file as a jumping-off place when direct entry is shut.

D4.outcome: In own games, rook placements are recorded with the target and entry square named in the review log.

misconceptions: Occupying an open file is a goal in itself.
Any open file is good for whoever has a rook available.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K20 (open files, the seventh rank, being first), K12
conditions: Rooks present and an objective exists (a pawn to attack or an entry square).
The file is genuinely open and the entry squares are not controlled.
A pawn-protected obstruction is undermined with a lever; an unprotected one is besieged with more attackers than defenders; sacrifice only after the quiet methods and only for the entry.
contrasts: An open file whose entry squares are covered by a bishop, so winning the exchange gains nothing.
Opening a file that the opponent's rook can reach first.
A closed file that will not open.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.BACKRANK.D1: the eighth-rank entry square is where a file pays off

note: Merged: POS.OPENFILE.SWITCH (restricted advance along a closed file, Nimz #9) is folded into D3 per MAP11 §3.
